analysis.one_liner: Permanently narrows which streams and wetlands are protected under the Clean Water Act.
analysis.headline: The bill to lock in the narrower 2020 water rule died in committee without a hearing or vote, having drawn 21 Republican cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently written into law a 2020 Trump-era rule that shrank the number of streams, wetlands, and other waters protected by the Clean Water Act, replacing a broader 2015 definition. Fewer protected waters means fewer federal pollution permits and checks on discharges into small streams and wetlands. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in committee until the term ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, the biggest gainers would be landowners and industries that discharge into or build on smaller streams and wetlands: farmers and ranchers, real estate developers, and energy and mining companies, who would face fewer federal Clean Water Act permits, EPA inspections, and pollution limits. Homebuilders and agricultural groups had long argued the broader rule imposed costs on ordinary property owners, and the bill's findings cite the burden on agricultural communities [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Locks a narrower, fixed definition of 'waters of the United States' into the Clean Water Act itself, giving landowners and businesses clear limits on which waters trigger federal permits, instead of a definition that agencies could change with each administration.

Reduces federal permitting and compliance requirements for farming, construction, and land use on or near smaller streams, wetlands, and seasonal waters, which supporters argued were being regulated as navigable waters despite being dry or isolated much of the time.

Restores a boundary the bill's supporters describe as the traditional one between federal water regulation and state and private control of land and water, ending what its findings call regulatory overreach into decisions that should be made by Congress and the states.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, people downstream would bear the cost: streams, wetlands, and seasonal waterways that lose federal pollution protection are the ones that feed drinking water supplies, filter contaminants, and absorb floods, and cleanup or health costs would fall on communities rather than the parties discharging pollutants. Landowners and businesses would also face uncertainty as courts sorted out the new boundary.

drawbacks.text: The narrower definition removes federal pollution protection from many intermittent streams and wetlands, which science and the 2015 rule's supporters argued are connected to larger waterways and supply drinking water for millions of people; polluting them becomes easier and downstream communities absorb the consequences.

Writing the 2020 rule into statute would freeze the jurisdictional line in law, preventing future administrations from restoring broader protections through regulation and forcing any change back through Congress.
The bill gives states the practical responsibility for policing discharges into newly unprotected waters, and states vary widely in willingness and capacity to do so, leaving gaps in enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real clarity to landowners and businesses about when federal permits apply, and its supporters sincerely argued that the broader rule burdened family farms and small property owners. But the main effect is to strip federal pollution protection from a large class of small streams and wetlands that feed the waters people drink, fish, and swim in, and the largest beneficiaries of that rollback are industries with discharges to permit — agriculture at scale, developers, and energy companies. A narrower version that targeted only genuinely isolated waters, with state backstops guaranteed, would have been a defensible compromise; this bill simply codified the narrowest recent rule, and it never advanced far enough to face that test.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 19, 2021, and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the same day.
The next day it was sent to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it stayed with no further action.
It was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never received a vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death in the sense of a new benefit, but the regulated industries it aimed to help — agriculture, developers, and energy — are better off than they would have been had it passed, because the broader federal pollution safeguards it would have rolled back never were rolled back by this route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated industries kept status quo protections

for.name: 21 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from the same party, providing its entire recorded support.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 19, 2021, and never scheduled a markup or floor action, letting the bill die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican: the sponsor and all 21 cosponsors were House Republicans, and the bill died in committee without any recorded votes.

industries.note: Agricultural operations would face fewer federal pollution permits and jurisdiction over farm ditches and seasonal waters, and the bill's findings explicitly cite relief for agricultural communities. Less oversight of discharges into small streams shifts water-quality risk to downstream communities.

Developers could build on or fill more wetlands and seasonal waters without federal Clean Water Act permits, lowering project costs and timelines. The tradeoff is loss of wetland flood absorption and water filtration that benefits nearby residents.

Narrowing federal jurisdiction would remove many waters from federal pollution permitting and spill-response oversight, reducing compliance costs for extractive operations. Streams and wetlands near those operations would lose a layer of protection.
The bill would shift which governments handle permitting and enforcement for smaller waters, moving work from federal agencies to states. Costs and capacity vary widely by state.
